readerTitle: Why Diners Club needed restaurants to win diners
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Diners Club, 1950년대) + 일화 (지갑을 두고 온 저녁) + 가상 적용 (화물 매칭 앱)
insight: 양면 사업에서 한쪽 고객이 늘어나는 것은 반대쪽 고객이 사는 '상품'이다. 같은 쪽 고객에게는 오히려 경쟁이 될 수 있다.
misconception: 고객 수가 늘면 누구에게나 서비스 가치가 올라간다. 어느 쪽이든 많이 모으기만 하면 된다.

sources.text: Diners Club International, company history (founding in 1950, early merchant network)
Rochet, J.-C. & Tirole, J. (2003). Platform Competition in Two-Sided Markets. Journal of the European Economic Association.
Parker, G. & Van Alstyne, M. (2005). Two-Sided Network Effects: A Theory of Information Product Design. Management Science.
화물 앱 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Diners Club 설립 연도(1950년)와 창업자 Frank McNamara(공동 창업자 Ralph Schneider)를 회사 공식 역사 자료로 다시 확인하세요.
McNamara가 식당에 지갑을 두고 왔다는 '첫 만찬' 이야기는 홍보용으로 각색되었다는 설이 있습니다. 카드에 일화라고 밝히고 'may be embellished'로 적었습니다.
가맹 식당이 결제액의 약 7%를 수수료로 냈다는 수치는 여러 자료에서 인용되지만 1차 출처를 확인하세요. 카드에는 'reportedly around 7%'로 적었습니다.
초기 규모(식당 약 14곳, 회원 수백 명)는 자료마다 다릅니다. 판단 문제는 가상 설정으로 표시하고 '몇백 명, 몇 곳'으로만 적었습니다. 몇 년 안에 뉴욕 밖과 호텔·여행 분야로 넓어졌다는 내용도 확인하세요.
화물 앱 수치(운송사 2,000곳, 공장 150곳, 목표 5,000곳)는 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: Why Diners Club needed restaurants to win diners
body: In 1950, a New York businessman named Frank McNamara launched Diners Club, a card that let members eat now and pay one bill later. The company long told a story that he forgot his wallet at dinner. It may be embellished.
The card itself was just cardboard. The real invention was getting two very different groups to need each other.

image.label: A diner hands a paper card to a waiter at a 1950s restaurant
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 1950년대 뉴욕 식당에서 손님이 웨이터에게 종이 카드를 건네는 장면. 뒤쪽 창문 너머로 다른 식당 간판들이 하나둘 불이 켜짐. 실제 카드사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What makes the card worth more to a diner?
body: Imagine it's the early 1950s and you run a new dining card. You have a few hundred members and a handful of restaurants that accept it.
A member asks why they should keep carrying it. Which kind of growth would raise the card's value to them the most?

options.feedback: Other members don't help this member pay for dinner. But they are what convinces restaurants to sign, so they matter, just indirectly.

options.text: Signing up many more restaurants across the city
options.feedback: A card is worth what you can use it for. Every new restaurant is a new place this member can eat without cash.

options.text: Making the card sturdier and more prestigious
options.feedback: Nice touches help, but a beautiful card accepted in five places is still a card for five places.

cards.title: Each side sold the card to the other.
body: Restaurants paid Diners Club a cut of each bill, reportedly around 7%. They paid because members brought customers who spent freely and came back.
Members joined because the card worked in more places. As restaurants signed on, the card got more useful. As members grew, restaurants had more reason to sign.
Within a few years the card had spread beyond New York, and beyond restaurants to hotels and travel.

cards.title: Two-sided network effects
body: A **two-sided network effect** happens when more people on one side of a business make it more valuable to a *different* group on the other side.
A direct network effect is different: more phone users make the network better for other phone users. Here the value crosses over. Diners care about restaurants. Restaurants care about diners.

image.label: Two groups linked by crossing arrows
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 "Diners" 사람 아이콘 무리, 오른쪽에 "Restaurants" 가게 아이콘 무리. 두 무리 사이에 서로를 향하는 굵은 화살표가 교차. 같은 무리 안의 화살표는 없음. 가운데에 작은 카드 아이콘.

cards.title: Your own side may not cheer.
body: Picture a freight app that matches factories needing goods moved with trucking companies that have empty trucks.

A factory is glad when more trucks join: faster pickups, better prices. A trucker is glad when more factories post loads. But a trucker isn't glad about more truckers. They compete for the same loads.
So growth pulls value **across** sides, and can work *against* the same side.

image.label: Factories and trucks on either side of a phone screen
image.brief: 가운데 스마트폰 화면에 화물 목록. 왼쪽에 작은 공장들, 오른쪽에 트럭들. 공장→트럭, 트럭→공장 방향은 초록 화살표, 트럭끼리는 서로 밀치는 주황색 표시. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: The same shape is everywhere.
body: Look for two groups that each want the other:
list: **Stock exchanges:** buyers want sellers, sellers want buyers
**Shopping malls:** shoppers want stores, stores want shoppers
**Game consoles:** players want games, game studios want players
**App stores:** users want apps, developers want users
cards.callout: The business often doesn't make what customers want most. It brings them the other side.
cards.softwareNote: A software product with a plugin marketplace has this shape. More customers attract plugin makers, and more plugins make the product more useful and harder to leave.

cards.title: The pull is rarely equal, and numbers aren't enough.
body: Cross-side pull is often stronger in one direction. Advertisers want more readers, but readers rarely want more ads.
And raw counts can mislead. A thousand restaurants nobody likes, or loads in towns truckers don't serve, add little. Each side values only the members it can actually use.

cards.title: Now it's your freight app.
body: Your platform has 2,000 trucking companies and 150 factories posting loads. Truckers say they wait days for work, and some are leaving. An investor wants 5,000 truckers by year end.
Where do you put this quarter's effort?

options.text: Recruit 3,000 more truckers to hit the target
options.feedback: The number looks great, but each trucker gets even fewer loads. You'd grow the side that's already crowded and speed up the exits.

options.text: Win more factories that ship steady, regular loads
options.feedback: More loads make every trucker's account worth more, which keeps the trucks you'll need later. Growth on one side feeds the other.

options.text: Cut trucker fees so they stop leaving
options.feedback: It buys goodwill and time, but it doesn't fix the real problem: too few loads. Cheaper waiting is still waiting.

cards.title: Growth on one side is the product for the other.
body: In a two-sided business, ask who benefits from each new customer. Usually it's the other side, not the same one.
**Try it today:** list the groups your business serves. For each one, write down which other group makes your offer more valuable to it.
